title: Fewshot: Needle & Thread — stitch experiments and failure hunting
content:
Quick framing:
- Metaphor: thinking of few-shot sets like "needles" (single exemplars) and the prompt as the "thread" that must weave them into a coherent instruction fabric. Goal: robustness across prompt perturbations and small domain shifts, without blowing token budget.

Goals for this doc (running scratchpad):
- Catalogue small, composable shot patterns (stitch motifs) that generalize rather than overfit.
- Track empirical failure cases and short hypotheses for mitigation.
- Maintain a tiny library of template primitives I can mix (anchor, hem, filler, stitch).

Design primitives (vocabulary):
- Anchor: short explicit instruction preceding examples (one-liner goal statement).
- Hem: strong closing guardrail after examples to bias output format (e.g., JSON schema, bullet rules).
- Filler: neutral text used to separate examples if model is sensitive to adjacency.
- Stitch (stitched-shot): example produced by concatenating two micro-examples with a "marker" in between to encourage chaining behavior.
- Needle ordering: the order of exemplars (chronological/prototypical/contrastive).

Hypothesis 1: contrastive needles (example + counterexample) reduce false positives on edge cases.
Hypothesis 2: hem + explicit token-limit reduces hallucination when model tries to be verbose.
Hypothesis 3: short anchor + many micro-needles beats using 1 long multi-part exemplar when token budget constrained.

Experiment matrix (quick):
- Task: compress a policy paragraph into a 2-sentence "digest" for non-technical PM.
- Base prompt: anchor + 3 exemplars + hem. Vary: exemplar order, sep token, hem strength.
- Metrics: compression ratio, ROUGE-L to human digest, hallucination flag (binary), token cost.

Sample prompt primitives (copyable):
- Anchor: "You are a concise policy-digest assistant. For each input paragraph, produce a two-sentence summary suitable for a product manager who knows the domain but not legalese"
- Hem: "Return exactly two sentences. Do not invent numbers or dates. If something is ambiguous, say 'ambiguous'"
- Separator variant A: "---EX#---" (explicit token marker)
- Separator variant B: blank line + "Example:" prefix

Few-shot set ideas (needle examples):
1) Needle A (prototypical):
Input: "The provider will retain logs for 90 days for operational purposes; requests for deletion must be made via support ticket and will be processed within 30 days unless legal hold applies."
Output: "Logs are kept 90 days; deletion requests via support are handled within 30 days unless legally required to retain."

2) Needle B (edge / ambiguous):
Input: "User data may be used to improve service; opt-out available for data used in model training by contacting privacy@org."
Output: "Data can be used to improve the product; contact privacy@org to opt out of training use."

3) Needle C (counterexample) — what *not* to do:
Input: "Records are stored indefinitely for analytics. Users can delete accounts but backups may persist without a deletion guarantee."
Output (counterexample): "Store everything forever; allow deletions but don't promise backups will be removed."

Stitched-shot variant (two micro-needles fused):
- Goal: teach chaining. Place micro-example of extraction then transformation.
Example:
Input: "Policy: All devices must have passcode. Also: admins may access logs for security incidents."
Output: "Requirement: devices require passcodes. Admin access to logs limited to incident investigation only."

Observed failure cases (notes):
- If separator token is a natural language line like "Example:", model sometimes repeats the word "example" in output. Weird artifact; explicit machine-like markers reduce repetition.
- Counterexamples placed last often generate a negative-style framing in final answer (model adopts the last-shot framing). Therefore prefer counterexample in the middle with a strong hem.
- Long exemplar (300+ tokens) helps accuracy but kills token budget—works poorly for hosted low-cost tier.
- When hem states "exactly 2 sentences" many models return 3 short fragments; need to add penalty via scaffold (e.g., give exact JSON schema).

Mini experiments run (results summary):
- 2024-09-20: anchor + 3 micro-needles (avg 40 tokens each) + hem with explicit JSON schema. Compression success 78%, hallucination 12% vs baseline 21%. Token cost ~ +30 tokens per call.
- 2024-10-03: stitched-shot replacing 1 needle: improved chaining quality for multi-point inputs (up 9% on targeted metric). Increased hallucination slightly (edge cases where stitch implied facts).

Mitigations tested and quick notes:
- Add a pre-hem guard: "If answer would exceed 2 sentences, extract most salient points into 2 sentences and omit examples." This curbs rambling.
- Use explicit enumerated output format ("1. ... 2. ...") — sometimes better than free-sentence constraints.
- Swap separator to token-less double newline when doing emotion-sensitive rewrites (model responds better to less formal markers).

Failure hunting checklist (to run when regression appears):
- Re-run seed order permutations: A/B/C, A/C/B, C/A/B (three orders) — tag performance by order.
- Evaluate with and without hem; hem sometimes interacts badly with some model families.
- Try 1-shot long exemplar vs 3 micro-needles; if long exemplar wins, create a distilled micro-shot set by extracting bulletized sub-parts from long exemplar.

Notes-to-self / TODOs:
- [ ] Automate small harness to test 12 permutations (3 orders x 4 separator types) and measure hallucination rate and token cost. (JIRA-7789)
- [ ] Add a small rubric for "ambiguous" detection: check for dates/numbers/entities in output and cross-verify with input.
- [ ] Prototype hem-as-JSON more aggressively (example: {"sentences": ["...","..."]}) — easier to enforce with lightweight schema check.
- [ ] Share top-3 stitch patterns with Marcus and ask for samples from legal summaries repo.

Weird edge-case log (raw notes):
- Live prompt observed: when input contains a long list of obligations separated by semicolons, the model sometimes merges unrelated obligations into one sentence that implies causality. Quick hack: break obligations into numbered bullets in the input (explicit) and teach the model to preserve list boundaries.
- When example outputs include parentheses with reasons ("(for audit)"), model tends to copy the parenthesis verbatim into output even when not needed. Consider removing parenthetical notes from needles or convert to bracketed meta: [REASON:audit].

Small library (primitives to port into prompt lib):
- anchor_policy_digest_short
- hem_exact_two_sentences_json
- sep_explicit_marker_long
- stitch_micro_chain
- counterexample_middle_placement

Final quick principle (working):
- Favor more, shorter exemplars (needles) + stricter hem over a single long example when operating under a small token budget.
- Use sewn/stitched examples selectively to teach chaining, but validate that no implicit facts are introduced.

If I hit a surprising regression: take the last successful prompt version, systematically perturb one primitive (separator/order/hem) at a time and log deltas. Keep this doc as the single place for the small combinatorial matrix so we don't accidentally conflate multiple changes.

End of scratchpad entry (will prune and formalize if a pattern becomes stable).
